summary: In Greek mythology, Bryce (Ancient Greek Βρύκη; also Bebryce, Βεβρύκη) is one of the fifty Danaids, daughters of Danaus. Apollodorus lists her among the daughters by the naiad Polyxo and as the bride of Chthonius, son of Aegyptus by Caliadne. Apollonius of Rhodes and later ethnographers connect the form Bebryce with the Bebryces of Bithynia; a late tradition (Eustathius) makes her, like Hypermnestra, spare her husband.
etymology: Greek Βρύκη / Βεβρύκη; the Bithynian ethnonym Bebryces was sometimes derived from her name, sometimes from a hero Bebryx.

sections.heading: Danaid bride
paragraphs: Apollodorus places Bryce twelfth among Danaus's daughters by Polyxo. When the twelve sons of Aegyptus by Caliadne cast lots for those maidens, Chthonius drew Bryce. On the wedding night, in the mainstream Danaid myth, she received her father's dagger and slew her bridegroom with the other sisters who obeyed Danaus; Hyginus likewise counts her among the obedient brides.

A separate, late strand (not attested before Eustathius of Thessalonica) has Bebryce refuse to kill her husband, naming him Hippolytus — a mercy tradition that overlaps the better-known Hypermnestra and Amymone variants.

sections.heading: Bebryces and namesakes
paragraphs: Apollonius of Rhodes calls the Danaid "Bryce," and some writers took the Bebryces of Bithynia to be named from her; others preferred a hero Bebryx as eponym. The atlas id bryce-danaid is this Argive Danaid alone, not a Bithynian founding hero under the same stem.
